tip: Languages take στα (sta): στα ελληνικά (sta elliniká = in Greek), στα αγγλικά (sta angliká = in English).
Πόσο (póso) before a describing word asks 'how': πόσο μακριά; (póso makriá = how far?), πόσο μεγάλο (póso megálo = how big).
Prices use 'it makes': Πόσο κάνει; (póso káni = how much does it make?) is the everyday 'how much is it?'
No word for 'of' after amounts – the noun just follows: δύο κιλά ντομάτες (dío kilá domátes = two kilos tomatoes).
The article works as 'per': οχτώ ευρώ το κιλό (ochtó evró to kiló = eight euros the kilo) – no extra word needed.
'Three' agrees: τρία (tría) with neuter nouns like τρία παιδιά (tría pediá = three children), τρεις (tris) with masculine and feminine.
With several items the price verb goes plural: Πόσο κάνουν δύο καφέδες; (póso kánoun dío kafédes = how much are two coffees?)
μισό (misó = half) agrees with its noun: μισό κιλό (misó kiló), but feminine μισή ώρα (misí óra = half an hour).
'At' + clock time is στις (stis): στις εννιά (stis enniá = at nine). Hours count as a feminine plural, hence the plural 'at'.
Parts of the day need no 'in' – just the article: το πρωί (to proí = in the morning), το βράδυ (to vrádi = in the evening).
One o'clock is the odd one out: στη μία (sti mía), not στις (stis) – one is a single hour, so the 'at' word goes singular too.
Half past is 'and half': δώδεκα και μισή (dódeka ke misí = twelve and half = 12:30).
σε (se) + a time span means 'in': σε δεκαπέντε λεπτά (se dekapénde leptá = in fifteen minutes).
Days are feminine – η Δευτέρα (i Deftéra = Monday), η Τρίτη (i Tríti = Tuesday) – except neuter το Σάββατο (to Sávato).
No word for 'on' with days – the article alone does it: την Τετάρτη (tin Tetárti = on Wednesday).
Hunger is a verb, not a feeling you 'are': Πεινάω πολύ (pináo polí = I hunger a lot) – no 'am' anywhere.
Ordering just names the item: Δύο καφέδες, παρακαλώ (dío kafédes parakaló). A single coffee changes shape: έναν καφέ (énan kafé), not ένας (énas).
στην (stin) loses its ν before most consonants: στη δουλειά (sti douliá = to work). It keeps the ν before vowels and hard sounds like k, p, t.
σε (se) + τον (ton) fuse into στον (ston) with masculine nouns: πάω στον φούρνο (páo ston foúrno = I go to the bakery).
Some verbs only exist in the -ομαι (-ome) form: έρχομαι (érchome = I come). The unusual ending changes nothing – the meaning is a plain action.
Negative future has a fixed order – δεν (den) before θα (tha): Δεν θα δουλεύω (den tha doulévo = I will not be working).
Liking flips the roles: the thing pleases you. Μου αρέσει ο καφές (mou arési o kafés = the coffee pleases me = I like coffee).
Liking to DO something adds να (na) + verb: Της αρέσει να μαγειρεύει (tis arési na magirévi = cooking pleases her = she likes to cook).
The event is a one-off, so δοκίμασα (dokímasa = I tried on); the description keeps the ongoing past: ήταν μικρό (ítan mikró = it was small).
'By herself' agrees with the person: μόνη της (móni tis) for a woman, μόνος του (mónos tou) for a man.
κλείνω (klíno) means both 'close' and 'book': έκλεισα τραπέζι (éklisa trapézi = I booked a table).
You ask a thing FROM a person in Greek: ζήτησα από τον σερβιτόρο (zítisa apó ton servitóro = I asked from the waiter).
χάνω (cháno) covers both 'lose' and 'miss': χάσαμε το τρένο (chásame to tréno = we missed the train).
After motion verbs, home needs no 'to' or article: γύρισα σπίτι (gírisa spíti = I returned home) – just the bare word.
A good time 'passes' in Greek: Περάσαμε υπέροχα (perásame ypérocha = we passed wonderfully = we had a wonderful time).
πουθενά (pouthená) flips by context: 'anywhere' in questions – Πήγατε πουθενά; (pígate pouthená) – but 'nowhere' with δεν (den).
The έ- (e-) in έγραψα (égrapsa = I wrote) only carries stress. When stress moves, it drops: γράψαμε (grápsame = we wrote).
Μπόρεσες; (bóreses = did you manage?) – the past of μπορώ (boró) means a one-off success, 'managed to', not just general ability.
γνώρισα (gnórisa) = met for the first time. Meeting up with someone you already know is είδα (ída = I saw) instead.
'To you' comes before the verb: σου έδωσα (sou édosa = to-you I-gave) – the little word lands in front.
The of-form follows the thing owned – reverse of English: το φαγητό της γάτας (to fagitó tis gátas = the food of-the-cat = the cat's food).
τη βοήθειά σου (ti voítheiá sou = your help) has two accents: with σου (sou) attached, stress would sit too far from the end, so a second accent is added.
One vowel is the whole difference: κάνετε (kánete = you do) vs κάνατε (kánate = you did). Listen for the a.
'Used to' is built into the verb form itself: έμενα (émena = I used to live) – no extra words needed.
στης γιαγιάς (stis giagiás) = at grandma's – the word for the house is simply left unsaid, like English 'at grandma's'.
ξέρω (xéro = I know) has only one past: ήξερα (íxera = I knew). Knowing is a state, never a one-off event, so no second past exists.
No 'about' after thinking: σκεφτόμουν τις διακοπές (skeftómoun tis diakopés = I was thinking the holidays) – the noun follows directly.
νόμιζα (nómiza) = I thought – usually a belief that turned out wrong: Νόμιζα ότι ήξερες (nómiza óti íxeres = I thought you knew).
σπούδαζα (spoúdaza) means being enrolled – studying for a degree. Tonight's homework is a different verb, διαβάζω (diavázo).
'Prefer X to Y' uses από (apó = from): προτιμούσα το βουνό από τη θάλασσα (protimoúsa to vounó apó ti thálassa) – 'from' where English says 'to'.
